newsitem.title: USA: Canada gas futures seen forging link to US market.
newsitem.headline: Canada gas futures seen forging link to US market.

text.p: A sluggish start has done little to dampen hopes that the New York Mercantile Exchange's Alberta natural gas futures will build a valuable bridge between the Canadian and U.S. marketplace, traders said.
"I think they'll be slow to join the party, but I think they'll like it," said one Canadian trader, referring to the contract's light volume during its debut week.
The need for a Canadian futures contract was long evident, since 10 percent of the gas burned in the U.S. comes from Canada, and 90 percent of that gas is from Alberta.
NOVA recently reported the daily volume of gas trading within Alberta under the NIT mechanism has at times surpassed 25 bcf and more than 3,600 separate transactions.
Despite the market's liquidity, volume has been light since the contract's launch Sept 27. Total volume for the first five days reached only 652, with 310 on the first day.
This pales in comparison with NYMEX's fast-moving Henry Hub natural gas contract, whose volume totalled 2,871 in its first five days of trade back in April, 1990.
Some sources blamed the lull on the fact that most long-term winter business had already been locked in by the time the Alberta futures contract was introduced.
"It came out too late. It will probably take about a year before we start seeing some big volumes," said one Calgary-based trader.
Before the launch, traders calculated Alberta gas prices using a basis to Henry Hub in Louisiana -- a big risk since market regions and factors affecting prices vary so greatly.
The new contract provides a direct correlation to NYMEX's Henry Hub contract.
"We'll also be able to do one-month deals, which we weren't able to do before," a trader said.

Because the physical Canadian market trades mostly on a term basis -- for example, Nov/March deals -- traders were left to pick a Henry Hub winter month as the basis for a deal. The new contract will help tailor the deal to reduce the risk.
Though most expect a smooth path to a successful contract, changing currencies could pose one obstacle.

"The real concern is the currency," one producer said, contending the contract should be traded in Canadian dollars per gigajoule, used in the physical market, rather than the U.S. dollars per million British thermal unit (mmBtu) specified by NYMEX.
The differing currency could lead to costly conversion mistakes, he said.
But others argue this is not a problem since most deals will be based off the Henry Hub contract, which is in mmBtus.
The futures contract will expire on the third to last business day of the month prior to delivery, as is the case with the newly-launched Permian Basin contract.
Also consistent with Henry Hub and Permian futures, trading of options will terminate on the business day before the last day of futures trading.
